opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few reasons, and some of them are a little surprising in hindsight.

The first is that proteins are fundamentally three-dimensional objects, and a lot of the early generative work treated them as sequences, as strings of amino acids, borrowing from language modeling. That works remarkably well for some things, but when you care about structure, about the shape of a binder or how a pocket is arranged, you really want a model that operates directly in 3D space. Diffusion turned out to be a very natural fit for that. You start from noise, coordinates scattered around, and you iteratively refine them into something that looks like a real backbone. That iterative refinement maps well onto how we think about structure: you get the global fold roughly right first, and then you sharpen the local details.

The second is that diffusion makes conditioning really flexible. In protein design you almost never want to just sample a random protein. You want something that binds a particular target, or that scaffolds a specific motif, or that has a certain symmetry. With diffusion you can fix part of the structure and let the model fill in the rest, or guide the sampling toward some property. That kind of inpainting and guidance is very natural in the diffusion framework, and it lines up with the actual questions protein designers ask.

Third, and this gets overlooked, the field had a strong foundation to build on. Structure prediction models like AlphaFold and RoseTTAFold had already learned very rich representations of what proteins look like, and they had worked out how to handle rotations and translations of residues in an equivariant way. A lot of the successful diffusion work essentially took those architectures and repurposed them as denoisers. So you weren't starting from scratch; you were taking a network that already understood protein geometry and teaching it to generate rather than just predict.

And finally, there's a data efficiency argument. The Protein Data Bank is valuable but small compared to internet-scale text or images. Diffusion models seem to do a good job of learning a smooth distribution over structures from relatively limited data, and they generalize in a way that produces designs that actually fold and work in the lab. That last part is what convinced people. It wasn't just nice-looking samples on a screen. People made these proteins, measured them, and saw experimental success rates far higher than what we'd seen with earlier methods.

So it was a combination of the right inductive bias for 3D geometry, flexible conditioning that matches real design problems, and strong pretrained structural representations to build on.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it comes down to proteins being a geometry problem more than a language problem. A protein structure is a bunch of atoms in 3D space, and the thing you care about is the relative arrangement — distances, angles, how a helix packs against a sheet. Diffusion is a really natural fit for that, because you can start from literal noise, a random cloud of coordinates, and iteratively nudge it toward something that looks physically plausible. Each denoising step is a local refinement, and that matches how structure actually resolves: you get the rough topology first, then the details snap into place.

The other piece is that the data had a shape that rewarded this. We have a few hundred thousand experimentally solved structures, which is tiny by internet standards, but the underlying physics is shared and highly constrained. So the model isn't memorizing, it's learning something closer to a prior over what folded matter looks like. And because you can build equivariance into the architecture — rotate the input, the output rotates with it — you're not wasting capacity learning that a protein is the same protein upside down.

And then the practical thing, which I'd say is the real reason the field moved so fast: diffusion gives you conditioning almost for free. You can hold part of the structure fixed and let the model fill in the rest. That turns out to be exactly what people in the lab want. Here's a binding site, build me a scaffold around it. Here's a target surface, give me something that fits against it. With an autoregressive setup that kind of partial constraint is awkward, but with a denoiser you just fix those coordinates at every step and sample the rest. It changed the question from "can you predict a structure" to "can you ask for one," and that's a much more useful question.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that proteins are fundamentally three-dimensional objects, and diffusion gives you a very natural way to generate things in that space. You can start with noise and gradually refine it into a structure, learning the constraints that make a protein physically plausible along the way.

That’s a useful contrast with thinking only about the amino acid sequence. The sequence matters enormously, but what you often want to specify is spatial: I need these residues arranged in this geometry, or I need a surface that fits against this target. With structure-based diffusion, you can make those constraints part of the generation process.

And there isn’t necessarily one right answer. Many different proteins could satisfy the same design objective. Diffusion lets you explore that range of possibilities. You still have to test whether the resulting sequences fold and do what you want experimentally, but it gives you a powerful way to generate candidates.

sol-6.1.text:
I think diffusion is a really natural fit for proteins because proteins are three-dimensional objects. You’re trying to generate a set of coordinates that obeys a lot of geometric constraints, and diffusion gives you a way to start with noise and gradually refine it into a coherent structure.

The other piece is that we had strong models for understanding protein structure already. So you could bring that understanding of what a plausible protein looks like into the generative process. Instead of having to produce the entire answer in one shot, the model gets to iteratively resolve the structure.

But there’s an important distinction between generating something that looks like a protein and generating something that actually does what you want in the lab. Diffusion is a powerful tool for the first part. Getting function right still requires experiments and learning from that feedback.
